idiom_name: master thread + N worker Threads over a Thread::Queue with sentinel shutdown
implementation_notes: Ruby provides the primitives but not the structure: Thread::Queue is a thread-safe blocking queue (push/pop, num_waiting, close) that acts as the work pool, Thread.new starts each worker, and Thread#join (or #value, which re-raises the worker's exception) is the master's join. The master pushes jobs and one sentinel per worker so each pop loop terminates, then joins; a SizedQueue gives backpressure when the master produces faster than the workers consume. Two language facts shape the choice: the GVL serialises CPU-bound Ruby threads, so real parallelism needs Ractor (isolated, shareable-object-only workers communicating by messages) or process pools (fork, cluster workers), and worker exceptions are reported asynchronously unless abort_on_exception/report_on_exception is set or Thread#value is used.
code_sketch:
queue = Thread::Queue.new
workers = 4.times.map {
  Thread.new do
    while (job = queue.pop)            # nil sentinel = no more work
      results[job.id] = compute(job)   # sub-service
    end
  end
}
jobs.each { |j| queue << j }           # master partitions + dispatches
workers.size.times { queue << nil }    # one sentinel per worker
workers.each(&:join)                   # join; Thread#value re-raises errors
pitfalls: The GVL makes CPU-bound worker threads serial and memory-hungry; use Ractor or a process pool when the sub-tasks compute rather than wait.
A worker exception is invisible unless abort_on_exception/report_on_exception is set or the master joins with Thread#value - otherwise the worker just dies.
One sentinel per worker is required; a skipped or shared sentinel leaves a worker blocked in pop and the join hangs.
An unbounded Thread::Queue grows without limit when the master outruns the workers (use SizedQueue for backpressure), and pushing after close raises ClosedQueueError.
